title: More Than Half of India's Fertiliser Never Feeds the Crop, Scientists Tell Kisan Tak Conference
excerpt: Crops absorb only 30-45% of applied nitrogen and as little as 15% of phosphorus, experts told the Delhi agriculture conference — and the remedy they prescribed was balanced nutrition and root-placed urea, not more bags.
body:
• At the Kisan Tak Bharat Agriculture Conference 2026 in Delhi, scientists and industry leaders said crops take up only 30 to 45% of the nitrogen farmers apply — for rice in eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Bengal, about 30%, meaning 70 kg of every 100 kg of nitrogen is lost.
  • Phosphorus uptake is lower still, at 15 to 25%, while potash reaches about 50%; the rest locks into the soil, escapes into the air, or seeps into groundwater as pollution.
  • The fix the panel kept returning to was balance, not more fertiliser: a roughly 70-year ICAR long-term study shows balanced nutrients keep yields and soil carbon up, and placing urea briquettes near roots could raise rice uptake towards 70%.
  • Urea's controlled low price is the distortion: the Fertilisers Association of India chief suggested bringing urea under the nutrient-based subsidy scheme and rewarding farmers who use balanced nutrition.

A farmer flicks a handful of urea across a field, and within days the leaves turn a deep green that feels like proof that more is better. At the Kisan Tak Bharat Agriculture Conference 2026 at Bharat Mandapam in Delhi, scientists and industry leaders described what happens beneath the surface instead: much of that nitrogen quietly escapes before the crop can use it, India Today reported.

The Numbers: Most of the Bag Never Feeds the Crop

Mahesh Girdhar, president of agriculture solutions at MAL, set out nutrient use efficiency — the share of an applied nutrient the plant actually takes up. For nitrogen, it runs at 30 to 45%; for phosphorus, 15 to 25%; and for potash, about 50%. The rest locks into the soil, escapes into the air, or seeps into groundwater as pollution. Dr Sudhanshu Singh, South Asia regional director at the International Potato Centre, put the rice figure for eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Bengal at about 30%: of every 100 kg of nitrogen applied, 70 kg is lost.

Independent research points the same way. A national-scale nitrogen budget study by Babbar and Balasubramanian, published in Communications Earth & Environment, found that only 50% of the applied agricultural nitrogen was converted into useful products, with the rest lost as reactive nitrogen — 17% as ammonia, 16% in runoff, 7% through leaching, and 5% as nitrous oxide — and estimated cropland nitrogen use efficiency at 56%, according to a summary of the study. India has pledged to halve nitrogen waste by 2030 under the Colombo Declaration on sustainable nitrogen management.

Imbalance, Not Fertiliser, Is the Culprit

Dr S. K. Chaudhary, director general of the Fertilisers Association of India, argued the problem is imbalance, not fertiliser itself. He cited a long-running Indian Council of Agricultural Research project on long-term fertiliser use, running for about 70 years, whose data show that balanced nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium — with secondary nutrients, micronutrients, and organic matter — does not deplete the soil: organic carbon does not fall, and yield and quality rise. Girdhar made the same point with a thali: a body needs rice, vegetables, and salad in proportion, and so does a crop, starting from a soil test, the crop's needs at each stage, and the target yield.

"We need nutrition, we do not need a seller."

— Mahesh Girdhar, president of agriculture solutions at MAL

Why Urea Wins, and What Could Change It

Farmers overuse urea because it is cheap and always available, Chaudhary said, and a sprinkle turns the crop green. He suggested the government bring urea under the nutrient-based subsidy scheme — which pays per nutrient for other fertilisers while urea's price is separately controlled — and reward farmers who use balanced nutrition. Placement matters as much as price: Singh said putting urea briquettes near the roots could raise rice uptake towards 70%. Newer products such as biofertilisers, biostimulants, and liquid and nano fertilisers could reach 60 to 70% efficiency, Chaudhary said — figures India Today noted are the industry's, so independent field data will matter.

The stakes are fiscal as well as agronomic. The Union Cabinet this week approved a ₹62,370 crore fertiliser subsidy for the Rabi season, as we reported in Cabinet Approves Rs 62,370 Crore Fertiliser Subsidy for Rabi Season — money that, on the conference's numbers, buys far less nutrition than it should. The panel also addressed crop protection: Ravi Hegde, head of global regulatory at UPL, said pesticides, like medicine, are tested to fix dose and timing and are meant to be used as directed, with pest surveillance and integrated pest management telling farmers when a field actually needs them.
